hero.eyebrow: College of the Holy Cross · Biology & Neuroscience
hero.name: Sant Lab
hero.role: Why can some animals regrow damaged brain tissue while others cannot?
hero.hook: One of the animals we study is the Berghia stephanieae, a nudibranch mollusc whose brain grows continuously throughout life and can fully regenerate — an emerging model system well suited to undergraduate-driven discovery. We study the role of glial cells — the nervous system's non-neuronal cells — identifying glial cell types across species and tracking how they change across development, aging, and regeneration.
hero.figureCaption: Berghia stephanieae develops from an egg mass to a reproductive adult in roughly eight weeks, with the brain continuing to grow throughout.

research.lede: Combining comparative connectomics, single-cell transcriptomics, and molecular neuroscience, we're identifying glial cell types across species and tracking how glia, progenitors, and neurons rebuild nervous systems across development, aging, and regeneration.

cards.title: Comparative connectomics
cards.description: Building a volume electron microscopy connectome of the Berghia brain with the Katz (UMass Amherst) and Lichtman (Harvard) labs, compared against Drosophila, mouse, and human connectomes.

cards.title: Transcriptomics & neurogenomics
cards.description: Mining single-cell transcriptomic data, validated with in-situ hybridization, to identify conserved and species-specific glial cell types.

cards.title: Computational image analysis
cards.description: Machine-learning-assisted segmentation and 3D reconstruction using open-source tools that run on undergraduate-institution-scale computing.

cards.title: Aging & regeneration
cards.description: Immunohistochemistry and proliferation markers tracking neurons, glia, and progenitors across development, aging, and nerve regeneration.

members.note: The lab doesn't require prior research experience or advanced coursework to join — first- and second-year students work alongside juniors and seniors, trying both wet-lab and computational work before choosing what interests them most.

closing: We combine connectomics, transcriptomics, and wet-lab work to ask how neurons, glial cells, and their progenitors change across development, aging, and regeneration — and which of these dynamics are conserved across the animal kingdom.
